english: One more kick; if Gonzalo Montiel scores it, Argentina is world champion.

At the halfway line, the captain stands hugging his teammates. Thirty-five. He has lost four finals with his country, and six years ago he retired from international football. And the Qatar World Cup final may be his last chance.
Montiel runs, and the captain looks up at the sky, which he points to after almost every goal, for his grandmother.
A quarter of a century earlier, a doctor in Rosario found that his growth had almost stopped, so he began sticking a small needle into his leg every night.
About four years after Qatar, Argentina played another World Cup final. Two days later he wrote a short message with two words in Spanish. Me vacié. Meaning: I emptied myself.
He was not much of a talker. He just played. So how did a quiet, tiny boy carry a whole country? It all began on a small pitch in Rosario, one afternoon when a boys' team was one player short.
In the message he also thanked his family; without them his career would not have happened. And the first to believe in him was his grandmother.
A small neighbourhood club called Grandoli, in Rosario, Argentina. Its coach Salvador Aparicio is looking for any player.
On the touchline stood Celia. She came to watch her grandson Matías, and with her was his little brother, four or five years old.
She pointed at the little one. The coach looked at him and hesitated; the boy was very tiny and much younger than the others. But Celia insisted and kept asking him to put him in.
Aparicio finally agreed. He put him on the wing near Celia and told her: if he cries, take him off.
At first he barely touched the ball. Then it reached him, he took it with his left foot and went past one boy after another. He did not cry. Years later he remembered scoring two goals that day.
In his first match the others were two or three years older, some twice his size. It did not matter.
Aparicio never took him off after that. And from that day Celia took him to every training session and match.

He is Lionel Andrés Messi. Born in Rosario on the twenty-fourth of June 1987, third child of Jorge and Celia. Yes, his mother is also called Celia, like his grandmother. His father worked in a steel factory, his mother in a small magnet workshop.
He has two older brothers, Rodrigo and Matías. Then the family was completed by a younger sister, María Sol.
Rosario is a workers' city on the Paraná, with factories and a port, divided by two clubs: Newell's Old Boys and Rosario Central.

The family lived in a simple house in the south of the city, in the La Bajada neighbourhood. He played with his brothers in the street until dark; he was always the youngest, and the one with the ball.
He went to a state school near home, number sixty-six. Years later a mural of his face appeared in the neighbourhood saying he is from another galaxy, and from this neighbourhood.
At home they called him Leo. Because he was small and very fast, his family and classmates gave him another name: La Pulga. The Flea.
His mother said he was a stubborn little rascal at home who hated losing even at cards. But on the pitch his stubbornness made him never give up on a ball.
His father and brothers support Newell's, the red-and-black half of the city. On match days the whole family goes to the stadium. And Leo knows where he will play.
At six he joined Newell's, his family's club. In an early match they won six-nil, four of them his.
The 1987-born group became a team people in Rosario still remember. They called it "La Máquina del '87", the Machine of '87. For years it hardly lost.
Sometimes opponents set a condition before kick-off: at six-nil the match stops. Even then Lionel got angry if he hadn't scored himself.

His coach Carlos Marconi told the story many times: he promised Leo an alfajor, a chocolate biscuit, for every goal. He scored so much that Marconi changed the deal: two pieces, for headers only. Soon the smallest player scored with his head and turned to him smiling, holding up two fingers.
His teammates remember details: before every match he cleaned his boots carefully and taped his ankles himself like a professional, at eight or nine.
A teammate remembers a derby against Rosario Central. Leo beat a defender again and again, until the defender's father shouted from the stands: kick him!
The league records credit him with more than two hundred goals in five years, and Rosario people think it was many more.
His size remained a problem: bigger defenders kicked him, and parents shouted from the touchline: stop him any way you can! He got up every time and asked for the ball.
His coaches tried to protect him and asked him to pass earlier so he wouldn't get hurt. But he kept dribbling, and if he lost the ball he went back to win it.
But in 1998, when he was ten, his grandmother Celia died. The one who had taken him to football was gone.
He later said she was a great love of his and it is still hard for him to talk about her. He dedicates his goals to her, and after many of them points to the sky.
His mother said that after Celia's death he talked to his grandmother and asked for her help. He didn't tell many people; he rarely talks about his feelings.
Without her he kept playing and remained his team's best player. But everyone saw another problem: the boys were growing, and he was not.
Newell's sent him to hormone doctor Diego Schwarzstein to find out why their best youth player was much smaller than the rest.
Tests showed he lacked growth hormone. Without treatment he would be ten to fifteen centimetres shorter than he should be.
One word followed him for many years: small. The best player of his age in Rosario, and the smallest.
There was a treatment: a small injection in his legs every night. But it was very expensive, more than nine hundred dollars a month.
He learned young to inject himself. Every night, a needle in his leg. A teammate remembers seeing him do it before matches as if it were nothing.
A friend's father taught him to drive on a quiet country road, at eleven.

Every month his father does the maths. The medicine takes a big part of his factory wage, and help from insurance and the club did not last. Without the treatment his son's football would end before it began.
So they looked for a club that would pay. Then Lionel had a trial at River Plate in Buenos Aires, one of the country's biggest clubs.
In 2026 Messi himself told it: he trained there about ten days, River wanted him to stay and even offered to pay for his treatment. But Newell's had to let him go first.
It was the closest he came to playing for a big club in his own country.
But when he asked Newell's to let him go, they refused, and River's offer was lost. He said: that ended everything. Then help came from across the ocean.

An Argentine agent in Barcelona received videos of a boy from Rosario. With another agent he showed them to the club, which invited him for a trial. In September 2000 Lionel and his father travelled to Spain, at thirteen.
At Newell's his teammates didn't know where he had gone. They were told he was ill.
In Barcelona he faced older boys, and sporting director Carles Rexach watched him.
It is said Rexach needed a quarter of an hour to get from his seat to the pitch instead of three or four minutes, because his eyes were on the boy.
At the trial was Cesc Fàbregas, later Messi's teammate for years. Before the match a coach told him to mark the Argentine tightly.
Cesc looked at him and thought he'd be easy, since he was tiny. Seconds later he was on the ground and the little Argentine was away with the ball.
Rexach said he told the club: sign him without thinking. But his bosses hesitated. The boy was foreign, very small and needed costly treatment. Weeks passed without a decision.
The waiting tormented Jorge. He had left a steady factory job and was living with his son in a hotel in a strange city, not knowing whether they would have a home there.
After more than two months, Jorge called Rexach and said clearly: if it isn't decided soon, we'll go back.
On the fourteenth of December 2000, Rexach met the two agents at a tennis club in Barcelona. With no paper, he wrote on a napkin a promise to sign Lionel Messi.
Club official Joan Gaspart later admitted: the napkin had no legal value, it was to calm a father about to leave. And it worked.
Rexach signed it with the two agents as witnesses. Years later the napkin sold at auction in London for more than seven hundred and sixty thousand pounds.
Barcelona paid for the treatment and gave his father a job. In February 2001 the whole family moved to Spain.
At thirteen Leo didn't understand what it meant. He only knew he would play and the injections would continue, paid by Barcelona.
For the boy from La Bajada it was a dream. For his family it was the start of the hardest year of their lives.
Nothing went as they expected. Rules on foreigners kept him out of official matches for months. And in his second youth match his leg was broken.
His mother, brothers and sister missed home. They did not settle in the city, so in the first year they decided to return to Rosario.
Jorge asked him if he wanted to go back with them. Lionel said no. Years later he summed it up in a sentence: I wanted to carry on, and my father stayed with me.
So the family was split between two continents. Lionel and his father stayed in Barcelona, living on part of his salary, the rest going to his wife and children in Rosario.
The thirteen-year-old was now eleven thousand kilometres from his mother, brothers and sister.
Sundays were empty. He played video games with his father in the flat, then, according to his biographer Guillem Balagué, cried into his pillow in his room.
Messi said: my father was always by my side, and we went through many hard things together.
At the club he barely spoke. At his first training the coach asked his position; he mumbled "forward" and sat in a corner of the dressing room.
His teammates were puzzled. Fàbregas said they thought for a long time he couldn't speak. He could, but he was very shy. He was not much of a talker. He just played.
They called him "el enano", the dwarf. But when the ball reached him, nobody laughed.

Little by little he found his place. His team had players born in 1987 like him, including Fàbregas and Gerard Piqué. They played with three defenders and always attacked, so people called them the little Dream Team.
Slowly the quiet boy began joking with his teammates, and they discovered his humour, his love of cards and video games, and that he hated losing at them as much as at football.
One season they almost never lost and Messi scored over thirty. And Piqué, much taller, protected him.

Their coach Tito Vilanova became one of the most important people in Messi's life. It is said they went three up in three minutes, and Tito joked to his assistant: what do we tell them at half-time, at eight-nil?
The injections went on every night, and he grew a little each year. By the time he was a teenager the treatment had done its job.
He would reach about one metre seventy, one of the shortest on any pitch, but tall enough.
His doctor in Rosario, Diego Schwarzstein, said: all I did was help a boy grow; Messi did the rest himself.
In November 2003, in a friendly opening Porto's new stadium, Frank Rijkaard fielded a sixteen-year-old youth player: Lionel Messi. On the other bench was José Mourinho.
It was only a friendly, but he played with the first team. That season he rose through four Barcelona teams, one after another.
His official debut was on the sixteenth of October 2004 against Espanyol. He came on late wearing number thirty, aged seventeen.
He was then the youngest player Barcelona had fielded in La Liga; others broke the record later. And he stayed at Barcelona seventeen years.
People at the club remember his extreme shyness; he hardly said a word. An agent said his legs were the thinnest he had seen on a player.
But one man in the dressing room knew his worth: Ronaldinho, the best player in the world, who embraced the quiet boy.

The other Brazilians looked after him too: Deco, Sylvinho and Thiago Motta. Ronaldinho sat next to him and invited him to the Brazilians' table. Leo said he learned a lot from them, and from him especially.
Not everyone was kind. Frenchman Ludovic Giuly remembers some senior players kicking the boy in training to see his reaction. He didn't complain; he got up and carried on.
On the first of May 2005, against Albacete, Messi came on late. Ronaldinho lifted a ball over the defence and Messi chipped it over the keeper. The referee gave offside.
Moments later Ronaldinho did exactly the same, and Messi did exactly the same. This time the goal counted.
Ronaldinho bent down and the boy jumped on his back. His first official goal for Barcelona. Ronaldinho is proud to have witnessed the start of the story.

Let's pause a moment. Something about me: I'm Kamil, I'm twenty-one, and I've been starting YouTube channels since 2014, when I was nine. Most failed. A hundred thousand subscribers and the silver plaque have been my dream since I was little. If this story means something to you, your subscription brings me a step closer. Now, back to it.
Spring 2006, Barcelona reached the Champions League knockouts and Messi wore out Chelsea at Stamford Bridge. In the return two weeks later he went off in tears with a torn thigh muscle.
The whole Camp Nou stood to applaud him, and Rijkaard put his arm around him. He was eighteen.
Barcelona won the final in Paris without Messi. He was so sad that he didn't celebrate. Later he said he deeply regretted that night.
In 2004 another question arose. Messi had lived in Spain since thirteen, and the Spanish federation wanted him for its national team.
Argentina's youth coaches moved fast: in June 2004 they arranged an under-20 friendly against Paraguay so that Messi would play it and be tied to his country.
Argentina won eight-nil. Messi said Spain had been possible, but his heart was in Rosario.
His old friend Fàbregas said Leo would have dazzled with Spain. Years later Spain won the World Cup without him, and Argentina waited eleven more years for the title.
At the 2005 youth World Cup in the Netherlands he was the star of the tournament. He scored six goals, including two penalties in the final against Nigeria, and Argentina were world champions.
He won the best player of the tournament award and the Golden Boot as top scorer. For the first time the boy from Rosario was crowned in the blue and white shirt.
Six weeks later, in August 2005, he debuted for the senior team in a friendly in Budapest against Hungary. He came on in the second half.

On his first touch a defender grabbed his shirt. Messi pulled his arm to free himself and it hit the defender. The referee showed a red card; he had been on less than a minute. According to reports he left in tears.
Years later he said what went through his head: I came on and they sent me off, and they'll never call me up again.
A teammate ran to the referee to argue in his defence. His name was Lionel Scaloni. Remember the name; years later he will return to our story.
And they did call him up again. In March 2006 he scored his first goal for Argentina against Croatia, and that summer played his first World Cup in Germany.
Against Serbia and Montenegro he came on as a sub and scored the sixth, becoming at eighteen the youngest Argentine World Cup scorer.
He also set up a goal for Hernán Crespo. He looked completely at home.
Against hosts Germany in the quarter-final, Argentina led, then the coach used his substitutions on others, the win slipped away and they went out on penalties.
Messi stayed on the bench the whole match, his first World Cup ending with him watching. He kept silent in front of the press; once again he was not much of a talker.
In April 2007, in the Copa del Rey semi-final against Getafe, Messi got the ball in his own half. He beat one player, then another, then another, then the keeper, and scored.
He set off from the right near halfway. In about ten seconds he crossed most of the pitch with the ball glued to his left foot.
Every Argentine knew this goal. It almost matched the goal of Diego Maradona, their greatest hero, against England at the 1986 World Cup. And Messi was nineteen.
Barcelona won five-two. But Getafe won the return four-nil and knocked them out. Even a goal like that did not save his team.
Hard years for Barcelona: Ronaldinho fading, the team losing, the club wanting renewal. Messi improved every month but was often injured.
In his message after the 2026 final there is another line: I swear I always gave everything. And it was true. But for years with Argentina it wasn't enough to win.
Summer 2007, the Copa América final in Venezuela: Argentina and Brazil. Messi is twenty, and Brazil won three-nil.
He played the ninety minutes and could do almost nothing, then watched Brazil celebrate.
His first final with the senior team. And nobody knew he would lose three more before winning.
In 2008 he wanted to play at the Beijing Olympics. Barcelona refused to release him, since the Games are outside the official football calendar. The case went to a special sports court.
Messi said the decision was his and the Olympic chance would not come again. The court ruled for the clubs.
But Barcelona had a new coach, Pep Guardiola, champion at the Barcelona 1992 Olympics, who understood and let him go.
In Beijing he scored two goals, against Ivory Coast and the Netherlands.
In the final against Nigeria, in front of about ninety thousand, he passed to his friend Ángel Di María, who lifted it over the keeper. It was the only goal. Argentina won Olympic gold.
He later said some things in football happen only once in a lifetime. It is his only Olympics and he counts it among his most precious wins. And in Barcelona a new role awaited him with Guardiola.
Guardiola surprised everyone with his first decision: he told Ronaldinho, Messi's hero, he was not in his plans. The team would be built around a twenty-one-year-old.
Ronaldinho left for Milan in the summer, after recommending his number ten shirt for Leo. And the quiet boy who once jumped on his back became, with his number, the team's star.
May 2009, Barcelona visit Real at the Bernabéu. A book by journalist Martí Perarnau says Guardiola showed Messi a video in his office the evening before.
Between Real's midfield and defence there is a gap. Guardiola said: start on the right, then come inside into that gap, and with the ball drive at goal.
According to the same book, Guardiola hid his plan until the last moment.
Messi played neither winger nor striker but in between, and defenders didn't know who should follow him. Barcelona won in Madrid six-two, with two goals from Messi.
Days later in the semi-final at Stamford Bridge, Barcelona were behind until the ninety-third minute. Messi passed to Iniesta, who scored, and they went through.
Three weeks later, in Rome, the final against Manchester United. Before it Guardiola showed a video of the season with music from Gladiator.
Before the final Leo remembered Paris, when he felt left out and missed the joy. He said: this time I need much more fun.
Seventieth minute: a Xavi cross, and the smallest player rises above the defenders and heads it over keeper van der Sar.
Van der Sar is about two metres tall, Messi about one seventy. And the very small one beat him in the air.
And Barcelona won two-nil.
That year they won everything: the league, the cup, the Champions League and three other trophies. Six out of six, which nobody had done before them.
The sixth came in December in Abu Dhabi, against Argentina's Estudiantes, and Messi settled it with his chest in extra time.
Weeks before, he won his first Ballon d'Or, the award for the world's best player, at twenty-two. And the very small one became the best.
In January 2011 at the Ballon d'Or gala in Zurich, the three nominees were products of one school, La Masia: Xavi, Andrés Iniesta and Lionel Messi.
Many backed Xavi or Iniesta, world champions with Spain, and Iniesta scored the final's goal. But Messi won for the second year running.
He said he hadn't expected it, and that Xavi and Iniesta deserved it as much or more. And they were the first to congratulate him.
The three held a press conference together and all said: the award is for the team.
Years later Xavi remembered meeting him on a trip: a polite, humble boy without arrogance. And he never imagined he'd become the best player in history.

In May 2011 at Wembley, Barcelona beat Manchester United in another Champions League final, and Messi scored with a powerful low shot from distance. The finest moment was at the end: that spring a tumour had been removed from defender Éric Abidal's liver, and Carles Puyol gave him the armband to lift the trophy.

In May 2012 Guardiola said goodbye to Camp Nou as coach. Messi scored all four and after the fourth ran to the touchline to hug him. Guardiola joked: Leo stole the spotlight all season, and I can't be jealous.
In December 2012 he broke a forty-year-old record: Gerd Müller's eighty-five goals in a year. Messi ended it with ninety-one, five of them in one Champions League match.

Müller wasn't angry; he called Leo a giant and joked: his only flaw is he doesn't play for Bayern. Weeks later Leo gave him a Barcelona shirt signed by hand: with respect and admiration, a hug. And Leo said: titles before records.
His life off the pitch changed too. His partner was Antonela Roccuzzo, a Rosario girl he had known since childhood. In November 2012 their first son Thiago was born.
Two months after the birth, Leo said fatherhood changes you completely, and his son now came before everything.

In January 2013 he won his fourth Ballon d'Or in a row, which nobody had done before. But Tito Vilanova, his coach since La Masia and first-team coach, was being treated for cancer again that winter. And Abidal had just returned after a liver transplant. In his speech in Zurich Leo forgot to thank them, then apologised. He said Tito believed in him when he was a boy mostly on the bench.
At Barcelona he was a legend. With his national team it was another story.
Argentina had not won a major title since 1993, when Messi was six. The nation was waiting for him to end the drought.
At the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, Maradona himself coached Argentina. In the Cape Town quarter-final Germany scored in the third minute and won four-nil. Messi did not score all tournament.
Maradona said he saw Messi crying in the dressing room.
And he added: whoever says he doesn't love this shirt is stupid.
And that's exactly what many said: he left for Spain at thirteen, doesn't play for an Argentine club, and doesn't even sing the anthem.
There was a name for people like him: "pecho frío", the cold chest, a player who doesn't get fired up when it matters. Many saw his silence as indifference.
At the 2011 Copa América at home, fans whistled at him. His father said his son was hurt and didn't understand why.
The coach at that tournament, Sergio Batista, tried to use him as at Barcelona, and failed. Messi said the comparison was wrong, as Barcelona is a team that has played together for years.
Argentina went out in the quarter-final on penalties to Uruguay, and the criticism continued. As usual he was not much of a talker. He just played.
In April 2014 Tito Vilanova died aged forty-five. Six days earlier, his assistant says, Leo visited him at home and they talked for hours. The coach of his first great team was gone.

Less than two months later, at the World Cup in Brazil, Messi carried his team. He looked at the sky after his goal against Bosnia, and scored four in the group stage, including a late winner against Iran in the ninety-first minute.
He was man of the match four times, and Argentina were in the final after twenty-four years.
In the semi-final they beat the Netherlands on penalties. Their defender Javier Mascherano said: without Leo we wouldn't have got here.
The final at the Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro, against Germany again. Messi and his teammates missed chances, then Mario Götze scored in extra time.
After the whistle Messi received the best player of the tournament award. On his way to it he passed the World Cup trophy and didn't look at it.
He said this award didn't matter to him. And Sepp Blatter, FIFA president at the time, claimed Messi kept telling himself: the best, not the champion.
It was his second lost final. Three years later he said: I'll never forget it.
At the 2015 Copa América in Chile, Argentina reached the final again, against Chile. A hundred and twenty minutes without goals. Messi scored, two teammates missed, and Chile won.
A month before, he had won the Champions League again with Barcelona in Berlin, with Neymar and Luis Suárez. With his club he won everything; with his country he kept losing.
Chile's coach was an Argentine, Jorge Sampaoli, and two years later he became Argentina's coach.
Afterwards Messi wrote that nothing in football is harder than losing a final. And he had lost three.
June 2016, another chance: a special Copa América in the United States, a century after the first, with the final at MetLife Stadium near New York.
The opponent Chile again. Again no goals, and again penalties.
Messi took his team's first kick; he leaned back and the ball flew high.
Chile won. His fourth lost final with Argentina, and the third in three years.
Lucas Biglia's kick was also saved, but everyone remembered the captain's.
Minutes later in the tunnel a journalist stopped him. The quiet one said a few words: it's over, I'm done with the national team.
His teammates were crushed. Sergio Agüero is his best friend, and they shared a room for years at almost every camp. He said the defeat destroyed Leo.
Messi cried on his shoulder for about twenty-five seconds, like a little child, repeating: this isn't for me, this isn't for me.
That night, the fitness coach says, he found Leo awake at two in the morning, crying.

Then something he didn't expect happened: Argentines demanded he stay. The country's president called him and said publicly Messi was the greatest thing Argentina had. And on a rainy Saturday in Buenos Aires, hundreds at the Obelisk held up signs: "Don't go, Leo".
And a fifteen-year-old Argentine boy, Enzo Fernández, wrote to him begging him to stay. Six years later he played with him in the World Cup final.
The country that had called him cold now wanted him back. Less than two months later he announced his return, and scored in the first match.
Asked why he came back, he said he loves his country and this shirt very much and wanted to help.
Later he explained why he'd wanted to leave: not just the pain of losing, but things off the pitch that hurt him and his family.
He said he doesn't remember whether he told his father before saying it in the tunnel. He just felt it was the right thing to do.
That summer a Spanish court convicted Messi and his father of tax evasion on his image rights, and replaced prison with a fine, as is usual for a first offence.
Messi told the court his father managed the money. The family had paid back about five million euros.

In June 2017 Leo married Antonela in Rosario, where they grew up. He could have married anywhere, but chose home. About two hundred and fifty guests attended, including teammates from Barcelona and the national team. In the front row were Thiago and his brother Mateo, and his brothers and sister were witnesses.
On the pitch, before the last round of 2018 qualifying, Argentina weren't even among the qualifiers. They had to win in Quito in the Andes, where they hadn't won in sixteen years.

That night Argentina's streets were empty, people in cafés and homes. In La Plata, U2 delayed their concert so fans could watch the match on screens. Then Ecuador scored in the first minute and everyone went silent.
Then Messi scored a hat-trick: three-one, and Argentina to Russia. Even Ecuadorians applauded him.
The players sang in the dressing room against their critics. Mascherano said: missing out would have ended many careers.
Messi said Argentina missing the World Cup would have been madness. Now they were relieved.
And their coach Sampaoli said an unforgettable line: Messi doesn't owe Argentina a World Cup; football owes him one.
Russia didn't repay the debt: against Iceland Messi missed a penalty.
It was saved by Hannes Halldórsson, goalkeeper and film director, who said he had studied Messi's penalties beforehand.
Then they lost to Croatia three-nil, and beat Nigeria with a Messi goal, and he was very relieved.
In the round of 16 against France in Kazan, Antonela brought Thiago and Mateo with "Papá" on their shirts. They lost four-three, and Messi went home disappointed again.

In his 2026 farewell message he wrote that leaving the national team was a decision that hurt him and still hurts deep inside. He had felt that pain before, at Barcelona. And there the end began on European nights the club wants to forget.
The cracks began. In 2018 Barcelona beat Roma easily, then lost in Rome three-nil. A year later it happened again: they beat Liverpool three-nil at home, then lost there four-nil.
Days after Anfield he said the coach was not to blame, but he and his teammates first.
In 2019 he won his sixth Ballon d'Or, a record, but it didn't fix what was collapsing.
In August 2020 in Lisbon, Bayern beat Barcelona eight-two.
Ten days after Lisbon, Messi formally wrote to the club: he wanted to leave. Barcelona refused; his contract didn't allow it.
His father flew to Barcelona to negotiate. In the end he decided to stay one more year; he would not sue the club he loves.
About six weeks later Barcelona let go of Luis Suárez, one of his closest friends. Leo wrote that he deserved a proper farewell, not to be kicked out like that. But nothing surprised him anymore.
Then in November 2020 Maradona died, and Argentina mourned for days. The man who defended Messi after Cape Town was gone, and the country still hadn't won a major tournament with Messi.
The pandemic shut the world that year. In summer 2021 the Copa América was moved to Brazil at the last minute, and the final at the Maracanã against them.
Because of the pandemic the stands were almost empty. He would play one of his most important matches with Argentina in silence.
The players had been away from their families for weeks. Before the final, in the dressing room, the captain of few words stood up, and someone filmed him.
For years people said he was too quiet to be a captain. That night he found his voice.

He told them: forty-five days without our families, lads. He mentioned goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez, who had become a father and hadn't yet held his daughter. And he finished: let's go out with confidence and calm, and we'll take it home.
Martínez said he wanted to cry. Another player said he cried a moment later and doesn't remember the rest.
In the twenty-second minute De Paul sent a long ball to Di María, the gold-medal scorer from Messi's pass. He lifted it over the keeper: one-nil.
For seventy minutes Brazil attacked and Argentina held on. Messi missed a chance for a second, and it didn't matter.
At the final whistle Messi fell to his knees and covered his face with his hands. His teammates ran and jumped on him until he disappeared beneath them.
He phoned his wife and children in Rosario. After four lost finals he was finally crowned with the senior team, at thirty-four.
Di María said the curse had to break one day, and it did. Messi dedicated the title to his family, the Argentine people and Maradona, who is surely cheering them on wherever he is.
A month later he was going to sign a new contract with Barcelona. But the club couldn't keep him, because of its debts and the league rules.
On the eighth of August 2021 he entered a hall at Camp Nou to say goodbye, and before saying a word he cried.
He wasn't ready and wanted to stay with his family. He came at thirteen and leaves at thirty-four, with three sons born here: Thiago, Mateo and Ciro.
He was sad he couldn't say goodbye to the fans in the stadium; because of the pandemic he hadn't seen them for a year and a half.
He signed for Paris Saint-Germain, and it didn't work. When the team lost they whistled at him.
Once, after a defeat, he travelled to Saudi Arabia on a promotional trip without the club's permission. Paris suspended him, and he apologised in a video. It was clear he wouldn't stay.
In November 2022 Argentina entered the Qatar World Cup unbeaten in thirty-six matches. Its coach Scaloni, the one who defended him in Budapest. Messi was thirty-five, and it might be his last chance.
He opened the scoring with a penalty against Saudi Arabia. Then Saudi Arabia scored twice in five minutes and won two-one. One of the World Cup's biggest upsets.
Messi came out to the journalists: no excuses. The dressing room is silent. But he asked Argentines to trust the team: we will be more united than ever.
The players said he started talking to them a lot. The quiet captain leading with his voice.
A song called Muchachos went with them. They sang it on the bus and in the dressing room, and Messi sang with them.
From then on every match was a final. Messi scored first against Mexico, and they won two-nil. Then Poland and Australia.
Against Australia he played his thousandth match, and scored in it.
They led the Netherlands two-nil in the quarter-final, and the Dutch equalised in the last seconds. Then Argentina won on penalties.
Then the world saw a different Messi. In a TV interview a Dutch player walked past, and he said to him in Rosario street slang: "What are you looking at, idiot?"
The one they called cold caught fire. In the semi-final, three-nil over Croatia: a Messi penalty, then he dribbled past one of the world's best young defenders and set up a goal for Álvarez.
On the eighteenth of December 2022, the final against France. A Messi penalty, then a goal by Di María.
Two-nil. Ten minutes left. Four finals behind him, and the trophy in front of him.
Then Mbappé scored twice in under two minutes: two-two.
Extra time. Messi scored: three-two. Then Mbappé equalised with a penalty. Three-three.
In the last minute Martínez blocked a French chance with his leg. After a hundred and twenty minutes came penalties.
Messi scored his. Martínez saved one, and France missed another. Then came Montiel, with the title kick.
This is the moment the film began with. Montiel steps up. Messi looked at the sky and said he asked God to end it.
Montiel scored. And Lionel Messi knelt on the grass.
He had lost four finals. He said: it's over. Then he came back. And now, at thirty-five, world champion.
Before lifting the trophy, the Emir of Qatar placed a traditional black robe on his shoulders. Then he lifted it, kissed it and wouldn't let go.
Then his family came down. His mother hugged him, his sons ran to him, and he photographed Antonela holding the trophy.

His two goals in the final took his tally to seven. And he won for the second time the best player of the tournament award, which hadn't mattered to him eight years before because of the defeat. Now the trophy came with it.
At that World Cup he became the first to score in the group stage, round of 16, quarter-final, semi-final and final.
He later said he heard the trophy calling him, as if saying: now you can touch me.
He said he had only watched the highlights of the final. And that his sons imitate goalkeeper Martínez's celebrations.
In Buenos Aires millions filled the streets, the team bus couldn't move, and the players were taken by helicopter.

In March 2023, before leaving Europe, he had another happy night in Buenos Aires. In the champions' first home match, against Panama at the Monumental, he scored his eight-hundredth goal. He said he had always dreamed of celebrating like this, in his country.

That summer his Paris contract ended, and he chose something that surprised everyone. Not Barcelona, not Saudi Arabia's huge offer, but young American club Inter Miami. People thought he wanted to rest.
He explained it simply: he wanted to step a little away from the spotlight and take care of his family. If he wanted money he'd have gone to Saudi Arabia.
July 2023, first match for Miami, he came on as a sub. With the score level in the ninety-fourth minute, he curled a free kick into the corner.
He smiled from the bench at Antonela and their children in the stands. LeBron James and Serena Williams were there. And at the goal, David Beckham, the club's co-owner, cried.
Weeks later Miami won the first trophy in its history. Is this rest? And in October, his eighth Ballon d'Or.
In Miami he became the father of young players. His three sons joined the club's academy, and he cheers them with Antonela like any dad.
Argentina reached the 2024 Copa América final against Colombia in Miami. In the second half he twisted his ankle and went off.
On the bench he cried. Paredes, next to him, said he couldn't look at him, he just heard him crying. Argentina won in extra time without him, in his friend Di María's last match.

In September 2025 he played what he said was probably his last qualifier at home, against Venezuela in Buenos Aires. In the warm-up he barely held back tears, with more than eighty thousand chanting his name. He scored twice and said: this is how I dreamed of finishing, in my country.
In December 2025 Miami won its first MLS Cup. His son Mateo played ball and pointed at his father.
In March 2026 he scored his nine-hundredth goal. He was thirty-eight, and people said he had got old.
It came in a match Miami didn't win, so they went out of a continental tournament. The result matters more to him than the record. And the World Cup is near.
His father Jorge always hoped to see him at another World Cup. But just before the tournament Jorge became seriously ill. For the first time he would not be there to watch him.
First, a hat-trick against Algeria. Then two goals against Austria and one against Jordan. They easily topped their group.
And after every match: take off the boots. Pick up the phone. Any message from home? That's how he knows how his father is.
He didn't say it then, but he played with his father ill thousands of kilometres away. He later admitted he wasn't okay.
Every knockout match a battle. Against Cape Verde, extra time.
Against Egypt he missed a penalty and didn't hang his head. He set up a goal for Romero, equalised, then Enzo Fernández headed the winner. Against Switzerland, extra time.
Boots. Phone. Message from home?
In the semi-final in Atlanta England went ahead. Argentina turned it around in the last five minutes, with a Messi cross in the last minute: two-one. And into the final.
After the match Messi was overcome by emotion. Then he went around the pitch hugging the players and staff. And Scaloni speechless.
He scored eight goals at that tournament. Nobody in World Cup history has scored or played more than him.
The final was on the nineteenth of July 2026, at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. Where ten years earlier he had said: it's over.
Before the match he asked his teammates to stay calm, forget everything and just play.
Spain had nineteen-year-old Lamine Yamal and a young team. They dominated possession and chances.
The score still nil-nil. In a video released later, Messi says: character, lads, character.
At the end of normal time Enzo, the one with that message, was sent off. Ten players, and thirty minutes of holding on.
In the hundred-and-sixth minute Ferran Torres scored, and no reply.
Messi had only one shot. His fifth lost final with Argentina.
After the whistle Messi sat on the grass. Yamal came and hugged him, and he told him: go on your way, the future belongs to your generation. Yamal said his words were worth a gold medal to him.
Scaloni broke down at his press conference and left the room. Before the final he had said Messi was the best ever to step on a pitch.
The next day Messi wrote to the fans: the pain is enormous, and the wound needs time to heal.
Less than three weeks later, in August 2026, Jorge died in Rosario after a long illness, aged sixty-eight.
Days later Lionel wrote him a letter and published it to the world. It began with a simple sentence: I love you, Dad.

He wrote that he promised his father to reach the final so he could come and watch, but his father couldn't. He wanted to win and bring the trophy to him, but he couldn't. There was nothing left in his legs.
He wrote that at the World Cup, after every match, he waited for a message from his father. And when none came, he understood how bad things were.
He wrote: you were my father, my friend and my agent. He was the one who left his job in Rosario and waited in Barcelona for a napkin.
And since that day there are two in the sky.
On the thirty-first of August he published the message from the start of the film. He had written it two days after the final and kept it hidden six weeks.

In it he said goodbye to the national team. He wrote: Me vacié. Meaning: I emptied myself. I have nothing left to give, and there are wonderful young players who deserve their place. Now I'll be one of you.
At the end he added later: today, after what happened to my father, I am even surer of my decision.
He didn't write about titles or finals, but about his family, the fans and his father.

On the sixth of October 2026 he played his last match for Argentina, a friendly against Benin at the Monumental in Buenos Aires. River Plate's stadium, which the boy from Rosario wanted and never got.
About eighty-five thousand came. He walked out holding the hands of his three sons, and his mother in the stands.
The anthem was sung by a veteran of the Falklands War, as Messi held back tears. In the tenth minute play stopped for a long ovation, and the Benin players came to him.
He set up two goals and scored a penalty: his hundred-and-twenty-sixth goal, in his two-hundred-and-eighth match.
The second was by Nico Paz, twenty-two, one of the young players he meant.
Hundreds of drones lit up the sky. And the silent boy in the dressing-room corner took the microphone in front of eighty-five thousand.
The first thing he said was that he was thinking of his father. Then he said it was the saddest day of his career.
For weeks people argued about the World Cup referees, and Messi stayed silent. That night he said: nothing strange happened, our team gave everything.
He said playing for Argentina is the most beautiful thing that can happen, and he wishes he could stay here forever. Then he told the fans: I love you, and I'll miss you.
Then he went around the pitch with his wife and sons, while eighty-five thousand sang that Messi won't leave.
He said it was the saddest day of his career. And yet in his message he wrote: I leave in peace, and I leave proud.
He was too small. Too expensive. A foreigner in Spain, and a stranger in Argentina. Then they said: he's got old.
But two people never thought so. A grandmother who told a coach: put him on. And a father who found the money, crossed the ocean with him, and stayed.
He didn't play only for himself, but for them. And when he looks at the sky after a goal, he is looking for them.
The cold chest they talked about was never cold. He just hid his feelings, and only let them out when he lost, or finally won.
And that last final, in July 2026, hurt him more than any other. It wasn't just a title; it was a last gift for his father.
And today he still plays in Miami, with more than nine hundred goals. He no longer plays for Argentina. He has become, as he wrote, just a fan.
Maybe among you is the quiet one. In the corner. The one they think doesn't care.
Leo was that boy. He never became loud, and he was not much of a talker. He just played, for those who believed in him. And at the most important moment he found his voice, and the world listened.
So if you are quiet, there's no need to be loud. Play. Your time to speak will come.
And on the farewell night, the boy who didn't speak smiled at eighty-five thousand: I talk more than ever, and I don't want to leave.
That summer Spain didn't only end Leo's last World Cup. Two weeks before, in Texas, it ended the dream of a boy who wanted the trophy just like him.
A boy from a small island in the Atlantic, whom his teammates called the crybaby. His name is Cristiano Ronaldo, and his full story is here.
